---
title: "Inclusion–Exclusion: Fix Double Counting"
description: "An interview maths technique with symbols, numbers and an independent proof."
---

## When this technique appears

When events, categories or divisibility conditions overlap.

## The question

**Why can't we simply add how many people belong to two groups?**

## Formula worth memorising

$$
|A\cup B|=|A|+|B|-|A\cap B|
$$

**Every symbol explained:** A and B are sets, ∪ means union or in either group, ∩ means intersection or in both, and vertical bars count the number of elements in a finite set.

**Substitute actual numbers:** There are 8 students playing chess and 6 playing football, with 3 playing both. The number doing at least one is 8+6−3=11, not 14.

## Prove the mathematical step

Adding each set counts intersection members twice. Subtracting the intersection once leaves every element of the union counted exactly once. For three or more sets alternate signs over intersections.

## Common mistake or limitation

The sets must represent the same population and counting units. For many sets the full inclusion–exclusion sum can grow exponentially in the number of sets.

## The 20-second memory card

**Memorise: Add individual counts, subtract pairwise overlaps, add triple overlaps, continuing with alternating signs.**

Practise by speaking the argument, not reciting the formula alone.

**Interview problems:** Count Numbers Divisible by A or B; Derangements.

**Research reference:** [See the underlying method](https://cp-algorithms.com/combinatorics/inclusion-exclusion.html). The worked examples and explanation are original.
